Comodulation masking release (CMR) is a psychoacoustic phenomenon whereby adding coherently modulated noise to an existing masker makes signals easier to perceive ( Hall et al., 1984 ).
A prevalent feature of natural sound is coherent amplitude fluctuations across frequency, termed “comodulation” (CM).

CMR encompasses two separate processes, dependent on the relative frequencies of the noise and the signal: within-channel CMR (signal and noise similar in frequency) and across-channel CMR (signal and noise dissimilar in frequency).
To quantify the effect of band-widening on the onset responses, we calculated across-frequency interaction (AFI; i.e., the change in onset response between the NB and broadband conditions).

value: Coherently modulated flanking noise bands greatly increased signal-evoked spiking in mouse A1, producing a neuronal correlate of true (across-channel) comodulation masking release, whereas simply adding incoherent flanking energy did not.
quote: However, coherent modulation of flanking noise bands produced large enhancements in signal-evoked activity, consistent with psychoacoustic measurements and corresponding to a true release from masking ( Fig. 1 D , G ).

value: The population-level improvement came entirely from neurons whose receptive fields were centred at or near the 20 kHz signal frequency, not from recruitment of off-frequency neurons.
quote: Thus, increases in sensitivity to the signal were largely restricted to neurons tuned to frequency bands adjacent to, and encompassing, the signal frequency.

value: Contrary to the equalization-cancellation account, ongoing noise-evoked firing was facilitated rather than suppressed when bandwidth increased, so there is no cortical cancellation of the masker at the signal frequency.
quote: Surprisingly, increasing bandwidth produced a significant increase in firing rate for both broadband (CM and IM) conditions relative to the NB condition across this population ( Fig. 3 ; sign test, CM, p ≪ 0.01, IM, p ≪ 0.01).

value: Ongoing noise responses during the signal window carried no information about masking release, ruling out active cancellation as the cortical mechanism.
quote: This demonstrates that there is no evidence of active cancellation (or reduction) of neuronal responses to noise at the level of cortex and the magnitude and relative change of noise-evoked activity in CM versus NB conditions during the signal window were not predictive of signal sensitivity.

value: Cells whose onset response to broadband noise was suppressed relative to narrowband noise (negative across-frequency interaction) were the cells that later showed strong masking release, making the early noise response a predictor of CMR.
quote: Interestingly, when we compared AFI values with CMR measurements in individual neurons (see Materials and Methods), we observed a clear pattern: cells demonstrating suppressed onset responses to broadband noise (i.e., negative AFI) demonstrated strong masking release ( Fig. 4 A , B , top row).

value: Removing the 400 ms precursor of comodulated noise sharply reduced cortical signal sensitivity, showing that prior exposure to the masker (priming) is required for large across-channel CMR in A1.
quote: Priming is therefore necessary to induce large across-channel CMR in A1.

quote: Selective optogenetic inactivation during preceding noise presentation caused a significant reduction in subsequent signal-evoked responses, demonstrating that auditory cortical processing is critical for large across-channel CMR in these neurons.
